doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Charlie Finley, baseball and medicine
summary: Finley, an insurance man who owned the Kansas City/Oakland team, becomes Budd's friend; stories of Gene Tenace and Finley's health.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: goodness he said the magic word. So he said when you come to New York I’d like to see you and we’ll go to a game together. We became great friends. And one evening, in Chicago, I saw him at an AMA meeting and we went out to dinner together with another doctor. We went to one of these places where they had dine and dance and a band played there, and I got to play with this orchestra for fun, and he was quite impressed about that. And he became a great friend and I’ve known him until the day he died. So that was medicine and baseball.
He owned one of the baseball teams, right?

At the time I knew him, he had bought the Kansas City team which then moved to Oakland. And he had an office in Chicago, and I’ve been there several times, and he closed his office business at four in the afternoon but at that time out in California it was only maybe two or three. He could listen and he’d talk, I remember him talking to Joe Kronin on the telephone and giving advice about things. And he had one day a young player from Ohio, Gene Tenace was his name, was a great catcher, a new player, and Charlie Findlay had another friend and I down to a fish fry in his office one night, and he had this young baseball player there, we met him, and Tenace — Findlay won three or four pennants in a row and a couple of World Series. And Tenace happened to hit two home runs in the first game or something, a lot of home runs, became quite famous. I’ve never seen him since, but I happened to meet that guy in baseball, partly through Findlay and partly through medicine. And also about health I know that Charlie Findlay had a coronary and had some medical treatment, not by me, but I saw him when he was sick in Chicago where he lived. But the three just seem to intermingle many, many, many times.
